utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to the OTP representatives, Ms. Dahl, Mr. Ferrara, and their team associates. Good afternoon, Mr. Seselj, and of course the -- good afternoon to the usher and the Registrar. We're ten minutes late in starting because the previous Trial Chamber was not able to stop at a quarter to 2:00, which causes this delay, because I was waiting outside the door at 14 past 2.00. I hope this is not to occur again. I have three topics. First of all, Mr. Seselj, your brief on the reply to the Prosecution motion for imposition of counsel has been translated. We have -- we got the English translation on Friday. The Trial Chamber notes the following: Your filings have two parts. The first part is under 35.000 words long, so no problems there. That will be admitted and filed. However, as to the second part, it is over 260 pages long, i.e., 91.000-odd words, so that will not be admitted because the title deals with violations of your rights. And I read the contents this morning, as early as 5.00 this morning. There's no direct relation to the key issue of whether you should be appointed a counsel or not. Therefore, the said document will not be filed. Something else, another problem. It has to do with the first document which will be filed. It mentions several protected witnesses, giving their names and pseudonyms. As a result, the version that you provided will be filed confidentially. However, as soon as you have redacted the first names and surnames, that version will be made public. The second topic. It concerns the witness we're going to hear today. The Trial Chamber handed down a decision on Friday. It is 11 pages long and has 51 footnotes. The document could not be translated into your language since Friday. I am therefore going to sum it up very briefly. It regards the testimony of Davor Strinovic. The Trial Chamber said that the motions by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 94(B), seeking admission of schedules B and C of the 18 September 2008 motion, including exhibits admitted in the Milosevic and Mrksic cases, those requests have been turned down, dismissed by the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, the Prosecution had sought to admit, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, annexes B, C, D and E of their motion of the 13th of July, 2006. They were transcripts of the testimony of the witness in the Milosevic and Mrksic cases and the exhibits related thereto. The Trial Chamber decided to dismiss that motion as well. However, the Trial Chamber authorised the new report to be added to the Prosecution 65 ter list. Therefore, the Trial Chamber, in its disposition, ordered that the witness appear as an expert witness. We recognise his status of expert. The examination-in-chief will be not over one hour and thirty minutes. As to the cross-examination, it will be 130 minutes maximum. The Trial Chamber dismissed the other motions. Now, regarding next week, experts Visnja Bilic is due to testify. As you know, Visnja Bilic is going to replace expert Ivan Grujic. On the 3rd of November, 2008, the Prosecution filed the report by Bilic pursuant to Rule 94 bis and sought to add this report and related documents to the 65 ter list. The report and the documents were provided to the accused on the 8th of October, 2008. The translation into B/C/S of the motion was provided to the witness on the 7th of November, 2008. The witness is due to testify on the 18th of November, 2008, so that's next Tuesday. And given the time limits for responses and replies, we have four questions for you. The first question: Do you challenge the additions sought by the Prosecution to the 65 ter list; that is, the report and the related exhibits? Secondly, do you challenge the status of expert of the witness? Thirdly, do you accept the report made by Ms. Bilic? Fourthly, do you wish to cross-examine the witness? So, Mr. Seselj, I know that you wanted to say something. You can answer the questions I put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, with regard to the information you've just given that you rejected the addendum to my response to the Prosecution and their request to impose counsel upon me, I'd like to draw your attention to the following: My response is less extensive than I was allowed. It's shorter. Secondly, along with his request, the Prosecutor attached material numbering more than 1.000 pages. I didn't even count them. Perhaps there are 2.000 pages attached, and it took up a whole box, a whole box full of material. My supplement to the response is four or eight times less than the Prosecutor's supplement to their motion, and I protest because you accepted the Prosecution response and not my supplement. Now, as far as expert Visnja Bilic is concerned, you will remember that I was opposed to having another expert witness called in, because Ivan Grujic was seriously compromised, in the professional sense and moral sense, in some other trials and proceedings, and Visnja Bilic appears as an uncompromised individual who will present his material. And as far as I was able to see thus far and look at the new expert report that was tabled, it is quite obvious that the report is wholly based on the material of Milan Grujic. Therefore, I am opposed to following the 65 ter rule for new exhibits and having this one added. I challenge the qualifications of Visnja Bilic herself, both in the professional and the moral sense. I do not accept her report, and I'm going to cross-examine her if I have the opportunity of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber is going to discuss what you have just said, and you will know as early as tomorrow what our decision is going to be regarding Ms. Bilic. Did you have anything else to say, because we're pressed by time today and I'd like us to move swiftly and hear the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I do have something to add very briefly, but three serious problems. First of all, it was the Prosecution's duty to disclose the complete transcripts of the testimony of Davor Strinovic in the Milosevic trial as well as in the Markesic and Mrksic et al trial. Now, in the Mrksic trial, they failed to provide me with 50 pages of the transcript, and I'm referring to the final portion of the transcript of the 23rd of May, 2006. Through the representatives of the Registry, I took up this problem with the Prosecution. I tried to have it resolved an hour ago, roughly, but was unsuccessful because I was brought here at 1.15, and so I wasn't able to resolve that issue, which means that it doesn't exist at all, because while I was studying this, I was thinking about it and I thought perhaps they disclosed it to me subsequently and I was just not able to find it. As the Prosecutor can't find it either, then that material just doesn't exist. So the person who translated this from the English to have it given to me probably thought that I wouldn't read through the whole lot and wouldn't notice that there are 50 pages missing from the central part of the document. But as I read through everything, I did notice it, and it's a serious problem. Secondly, and this will be even briefer, yesterday I received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the question straight away. Ms. Dahl or Mr. Ferrara, Mr. Seselj is telling us that he was provided with a transcript of the 23rd of May, 2006, with 60 pages missing. That's what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have just discovered what Mr. Seselj say when he informed the Court Officer, and he's right because they were not translated, the afternoon session of the evening of the 23rd of May, 2006. We immediately directed our office to translate these 50 pages missing, and we hope to disclose it to Seselj -- to Mr. Seselj as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you've got your answer, Mr. Seselj, to this problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I should have been provided it at least half an hour before Strinovic comes into the courtroom, whereas I'm going to receive it, I think, when Davor Strinovic has returned to Zagreb. So that's the problem. Had I not read through all this or had I had some unskillful counsel or lawyer, that would have gone unnoticed, you see. The second problem is this: Yesterday, I received a request for VS-35 on the basis of 92 ter, a request from the Prosecutor, and as the Trial Chamber you rejected that request. Now they're bringing it up again. And it is dated the 28th of October, but I was just handed it yesterday. I am categorically opposed to having this request by the Prosecution adhered to, and I would like to put forward all the reasons that I've already stated, why we cannot apply Rule 92 ter in these proceedings, so I hope I don't have to repeat all my points again. You know that I stated my views and presented the reasons and repeated them several times, so that's the second point. Now, the third point is this: Just before I entered the courtroom, I received a request from the Prosecutor for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding VS-035, Mr. Ferrara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably there's a misunderstanding interpretation, because VS-35 testified viva voce [indiscernible]. For this reason, it was Mr. [Indiscernible] Ejic, so --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.035, 1.035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was 1.035. Now, if the Trial Chamber has already dismissed the first request, request saying that it should be a viva voce witness, we now take due note of new filings. The Trial Chamber will examine them, but at first blush I can't see why we should change tack. But let's wait until we see the contents of the filing. Third and last point, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before coming into the courtroom, I received a Prosecution request dated the 26th of September, 2008, and the heading is "Request for formally taking note of facts relevant for the crime base with respect to Vukovar." And there's a large number of those facts set out in that document, almost 300. I don't have time to count them all. But, anyway, I'd like to inform you that I'm categorically opposed to that, too, regardless of the fact that certain facts are notoriously well known. So there was no reason to table this motion. They can be seen from the general context and from numerous testimonies and documents presented. However, there are some which are completely unacceptable. But, anyway, the Mrksic et al trial is still ongoing, that is to say, it is in the appeals stage, and they are not adjudicated facts. Adjudicated facts are only those which have been officially adjudicated. And so because of that very strong formal reason, this is completely unacceptable. I think some notoriously well-known facts are mentioned to cover up other things, but, to be honest, I haven't had time to read through the whole document because I had to enter into the courtroom. So for these reasons, I am categorically opposed to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't want to make any filings, or have you just explained orally why you oppose them? Do you intend to make any filings as to judicial notice?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I think it suffices for me to say this out loud in the courtroom and it to be recorded in the transcript, and that will save time, because I have filed more than 400 motions and submissions to date, so let's make matters simpler. If I have to write a filing, then I'll have to do it in writing, in my own handwriting, without a typewriter, et cetera. So while it's translated and sent to the Prosecutor, this will require a lot of time. But I've already stated my formal reason, and I think it is sufficient for you to reject it. And, anyway, of late I've been applying this kind of practice, that is, to respond orally to everything that I receive, because mostly the arguments I'd like to put forward are repeated, so there's no reason for me to write them all down. And I have to prepare for all the testimonies and just have two or three days free between one testimony and another, so I don't have much time to write submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well. Mr. Usher, can you bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you please state your first name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Davor Strinovic, 8th of March, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a physician, a specialist of forensic medicine, and a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in the subject of forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're a forensic pathologist. Does that mean that you do forensic post-mortems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I perform autopsies at the Forensic Medicine Institute of the University of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before this Tribunal? And if so, in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I testified on several occasions; in the Milosevic case, then in the Sljivancanin case, as well as in the Martic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was on three occasions. In your own country or in other countries, have you had an opportunity to testify to events related to the former Yugoslavia or did you testify only here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was once invited to a trial associated with the Ovcara case in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some brief explanations. I mean, nothing I'm about to say is going to be a surprise to you, because you have testified on several occasions. You must have met with Mr. Ferrara. He's going to put questions to you, following the report you drafted and documents related thereto. He's going to submit documents to you, following which Mr. Seselj, who's sitting on your left-hand side, is going to cross-examine you. It may be that the three Judges sitting in front of you also have questions to you. These are very technical matters, so please do endeavour to be very precise, and if you have the feeling that we fail to understand, then you can expand on your answers. This is what I wanted to tell you. Without further adieu, you may proceed, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Given the Court's decision on 7 November 2008, qualifying Mr. Strinovic as expert with respect to his report concerning the exhumation and identification in Ovcara, I won't be covering a tremendous amount of his background.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Very quickly, Dr. Strinovic, you say that you testified before this Tribunal in the Milosevic, Martic, and Mrksic trials. Were you asked to provide a new report in the case against Mr. Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked to present my current position in connection with this particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you have this report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 7250. Meanwhile, we can continue with the questions so we save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: With this report, did you provide to the office of the Prosecutor your updated curriculum vitae, CV?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the highest degree, including specialisation, you hold, and from what institutions you obtained this degree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said, I'm a forensic medicine specialist. After that, I obtained my Master's and Doctoral degree at the Medical Faculty in Zagreb and became an assistant professor and later on a professor, full professor, at the Medical Faculty. And within the last two months, I've also been head of the Forensic Medicine Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you are also a professor. Where do you teach?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I teach the subject forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your CV had mentioned commissions and congresses you have participated in. Did these include topics that are of interest in this case, so such as identification, exhumation, and cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Namely, after we started with the exhumations within the institute and then at state level, and gaining experience in that field, we presented our cases to the international public by publishing articles or by participating in congresses where we presented our experiences with exhumations and identifications, both classical DNA and other types of identification, and we passed on our experiences to the international scientific community, as is standard in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Have you ever written books or scientific papers on these topics?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said, we wrote scientific articles and also parts of books dealing with the subject of forensic medicine generally, and specific chapters dealing with exhumation and identification in mass disasters of the kind that war is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your own country, how many forensic pathologists are there? Are they to be counted in scores, or hundreds, or is it just a handful of you? How many of you are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true, Your Honour, Croatia is a small country with 4.5 million inhabitants. We have 20 forensic pathologists, of which 12 or 13 are purely specialised in this discipline, and others are pathologists and also specialise in other disciplines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are a professor in forensic medicine, can it be said that you are the number one in forensic medicine in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't put it that way. There are other professors who are retired but who cooperate with us always, but we do work in the number one institution in our state. That is the oldest and the biggest forensic medicine institution in Croatia, and I am the director or the head of that institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that you have some -- you have testified before this Tribunal in other cases. Did you submit any written report in that case, Milosevic, Mrksic and Martic trials?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I submitted reports in those cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you have this report in front of you? Your Honours, for your assistance and of the accused, is the report number 2672. That is the second document in the first binder. I will give you this reference along with all the testimony just for your assistance and for the accused.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Where exactly is this that your question is about?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: It is the second document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What is the answer that you require from me? I see these documents. These are my documents, I wrote them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you draft this report; yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: With your report -- this is the report in the Milosevic and Mrksic case, and attached to this report there are several tables related to certain localities in the former Yugoslavia, including Ovcara, near Vukovar, and Vocin. They are the only two localities involved in our case. Before you come to testify, did you have the opportunity to examine your documentation concerning these locations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I did have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Would these underlying documentation be available in your office in Zagreb, and could it be reviewed if the Court or the parties would like to do so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say the following: All the documents which are associated with the work that was done in the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb, all these documents exist at the institute in written form as well as in computerised form, whereas the documents associated with cases done by other experts, they also exist, but they are in the Commission for Missing Persons. For instance, a case in point is that of Ovcara, where we did not process or participate in the process of examining the post-mortem remains, and that is why those documents are not kept in the institute, as are those pertaining to cases that were processed by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: We have already said that you were asked to submit a new report for the case against Mr. Seselj. I'd like to direct your attention to this report that you produced for the present case. That is, for the assistance of Your Honours and for the accused, the first document in the first binder. That is the 65 ter number 7250, and of course I will seek to tender both these reports at the end of the examination of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Is that the report that you produced for this case, the first document in your personal binder? The first document, the tab 1. Maybe I was not clear.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: 7520, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is the 65 ter number. 7250, I'm sorry. I changed that one number. 7250.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Tab 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm unable to find that number. This is my material, that's for sure, but I cannot find the number that you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strinovic, it's the first document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document which I drafted for this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Just some general questions. Firstly, would you be so kind to define, in very brief terms, what is forensic pathology? Very briefly, of course.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Forensic medicine is a branch of medicine which deals with a specific subject matter. It is associated with medicine and traumas, primarily meaning all kinds of wounds and causes of deaths, and forensic medicine in fact serves to help translate medical subject matter to court language and thereby make proceedings in court possible. The basic thing which we do is to establish -- ascertain causes of death after post-mortems, i.e., for the needs of courts. Apart from the cause of deaths, the manner of death and also the weapons used. We also establish all other forms of violence which lead to the injuries of persons and establish the mechanism of the infliction of injuries. And that is the -- and those are the fundamentals of forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You mentioned in paragraph -- in the first paragraph of this report that in December, 1991 until now, you have participated in the work of the Croatian government Commission for Detained and Missing People; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Namely, at the beginning of the war, which is to say in October or November of 1991, we were faced, in the Republic of Croatia, with the formidable problem of a great number of missing persons, and the first thing we did in that situation was to set up a commission, the so-called Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons, which was to collect data related to what happened to such persons. So this commission started working in December 1991, and for a number of years, up to this very day, has been in existence, and the basic problem still remains missing persons. I have to note that today in Croatia, we still have a thousand persons who are unaccounted for and are considered missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So could you briefly explain to us the purpose of this commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've stated, the commission's task was to create lists of all missing persons. Then it was to get in touch with the families of the missing persons, gathering data on such persons. Also, the commission liaised with the then former Yugoslavia and later Serbia in connection with missing persons. It also had similar contacts with the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, trying in that way to collect as much data as possible that might facilitate the later work on tracing such persons, whether they were captured persons or dead -- killed persons, and to later also find their gravesites and identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the nature of the commission's work when the conflict was still in process, so between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, from 1991 to 1995 the commission had a theoretical, we can say, part of its work, which is to collect and exchange data, talk to other parties, and thus it endeavoured to create as large a database as possible from which -- upon which to draw subsequently in the process of identification, which only started in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the nature of the cooperation between your commission and the Yugoslav government commission in that period? Was it smooth or difficult?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that particularly in the beginning, namely, 1992, when these meetings were first held, they were always monitored by international organisations. They were very difficult and very scant useful information was obtained in the beginning of these negotiations. Later, the commission increasingly -- cooperated increasingly better with both the Serbian and the Bosnian sides, so that today these commissions are still in touch and are still cooperating, and that cooperation is much better. But talking about the beginnings, 1991 and 1992, those meetings were very difficult, and the results were quite meager.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that at the beginning of the war, it was established, this commission. Do you know if there was a specific event that set up -- that moved to the decision to set up this commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that there were a number of reasons for setting up this commission. Certainly, a war which resulted in such a large number of victims, with so many people missing and killed or in camps was one, but the decisive factor why already in December 1991 we set up this commission was the event which took place in the Vukovar Hospital; namely, over 260 persons went missing from that hospital, and nothing was known of them until the mass grave at Ovcara was found. Obviously, this incident at the hospital had a specific weight which accelerated the formation of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was your specific role within this commission and what it is now?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: My role in the commission then, in 1991 and 1992, was to collect and obtain data regarding missing persons, in cooperation with the Red Cross and the families of the missing persons. Also, we were to look for data that would be of interest for later identification, the ante-mortem data with characteristics of the missing persons, and in that regard it was particularly important to collect such data as early as possible and to get the best-quality data so as to facilitate our later work in the exhumation and identification processes. It was essential, from the medical standpoint, to get the best possible descriptions of the missing persons, to obtain all the ante-mortem data, namely, information that would assist us later in transacting our identification part of the work as quickly and efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Could you describe very briefly for the Trial Chamber the procedure of exhumation and identification, and what kind of qualifications were involved in this procedure?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Every procedure of exhumation requires preliminary actions, in terms of talks with witnesses and the identification of the location of the mass grave. In the majority of cases, it took us a very long time to find the mass graves, to find the places where the bodies had been buried. Once the location for exhumation has been established, then we would start with our preparations, meaning examination of the terrain to see whether there were any mines or any other devices that could compromise the exhumation itself. Then we would secure the site and start with the exhumation proper. It was done by a team headed by a physician, either a forensic medicine expert or a pathologist, and he supervised the exhumation, namely, the digging up of the mortal remains of the people buried there. The objective of every exhumation is to try, as painfully and -- painlessly and as efficiently to reach the body without injuring it, without -- and with all the articles associated with the body in question to be preserved along with the body, not to mix them with the articles belonging to other persons, i.e., other bodies. So the exhumation meant digging up the body, and once the body was presented, it would be individually placed in a body-bag, which would be marked with numbers inside and outside the bag, and the thus marked bag would then be further processed either in the -- at the site itself or in the dissecting room, where the conditions are of course much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: The exhumations that were conducted as a result of the war in Croatia, were they conducted by the Croatian government, through your commission, or were they also conducted by international organisations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, especially when larger mass graves were in question, international organisations did the exhumation and we were present there in the capacity of monitors. Also, the Serbian side always had its own observers attending such procedures at mass graves. When we took over the complete procedure of exhuming mass graves, an international organisation would always be present, so that practically throughout all these years, there was always an international organisation present when the mass graves in Croatia were being exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Concerning the qualifications that were involved in this procedure, can you tell us very quickly what kind of qualifications were involved in the exhumation, in the analysis of mortal remains and in the identification process?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is quite a complex question. I shall try to be as brief as possible and as clear as possible. The procedure of exhumation itself, for instance, in the Ovcara case was taken over completely by international organisations, meaning first anthropologists and archaeologists attended the scene, they did their measurements, and then after they proceeded with the digging, which was archaeological-type digging, meaning inch by inch, in order to completely and efficiently have such a gravesite presented, i.e., the mortal remains in it. When Croatia was in charge of such exhumations, we did not have archaeologists because we do not have such experts, and it was conducted by specially-trained people who did the excavation, the digging up, always supervised by physicians, i.e., by forensic medicine experts and pathologists, who saw to it that the exhumation was being carried out properly and at the best possible level at the given moment. That is as far as exhumations are concerned. As regards the subsequent processing, it was relatively the same, by international experts and by us in Croatia, but I do have to mention that not all cases were processed in optimal conditions, which is to say at institutes. A part of cases where we had a larger number of mortal remains, such as that of the Vukovar Cemetery, where there were over 1.000 mortal remains, the complete processing was done at the cemetery itself, where we had makeshift tents and makeshift conditions for such work, and the forensic experts, the forensic medical experts, with the help of technicians, processed the mortal remains there in-situ, and the identification was also done at that location, because we invited the families of the exhumed persons to attend the site and we were able to identify most of the bodies. The bodies had been well preserved, so that identification in the field was possible. In all complex cases of identification, namely, when much time has elapsed since death and where the bodies were damaged or heaped in piles, the identification was done in adequate institutions where -- and the majority of the cases were processed at the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb where, first of all, there was an X ray machine and every body was X-rayed, every single body was X-rayed to ascertain any changes that might indicate the causes of death or possibly facilitate identification, such as the existence of prostheses or metal objects in the body that could assist us in this identification procedure. After the X-raying of every single body, the forensic medicine expert would start his processing, assisted by an anthropologist who would ascertain on the basis of the bones the stature, the height, the age of that person, such persons, and also help establish the cause of death. Then there was the dentist, who inspected the complete status and established the complete status of the teeth, also to aid later identification. So that after such processing, a sample of the teeth or of the bones would be taken for DNA analysis, and thereby such a procedure would be completed in terms of the processing of the mortal remains. That data obtained in this way, by this post-mortem, could then be compared with the previously-collected ante-mortem data which we collected since 1995, which then all together would facilitate the identification. So we had the post-mortem procedure in the room itself, plus the data obtained previously -- would be compared to the data obtained previously, and that is how we were able to identify the mortal remains. That was the so-called classical method of identification when, by collecting all relevant data, the age, the sex, the height, the stature, the status of the teeth, different damage and disease on the body itself, possibly some medical interventions that could be seen, objects, articles, documents, all those were collected and were of relevance, and all these made it possible for us to compare all these elements with the ante-mortem data obtained from the relatives and family, on which basis we then made a classical identification, which in 80 per cent of the -- which is the manner in which 80 per cent of the identifications in Croatia were made. When this was impossible to do this way, we performed a DNA analysis, which only started to be applied as of the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why did you start only in 2000?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, the DNA analysis -- well, there's a new method there, a new method in the world that started in the 1990s, but it was only experimental. But then in practice, it was only at the end of the 1990s and the beginning of the year 2000 when the method became more prominent, and so we started using it. And we included DNA analysis, which was able to give us 100 per cent certainty the identity of an individual, and so on and so forth. And I can explain this. Samples of the bone tissue or teeth were taken from the deceased person, and then the DNA is isolated from the samples, and then that DNA is compared to the blood of relatives. Parents is best, or the wife and child -- her mother and child. And then with 99 per cent certainty, we can establish who the person is, the identity of the person. The DNA analysis is of great assistance to us in our work, although there are cases where that doesn't help too, and it doesn't help in carbonised bodies, that is to say, bodies that have been completely burned, or when the bones are too small, too minute, and have laid on the surface of the soil and are damaged or dried out, so bones of that type cannot be used for DNA analysis. So as I say, although DNA analysis is a very good method, we're not able to use it in all cases. There are cases where we have no relatives to go by to compare the samples and to take blood from, and therefore we're not able to establish identity. So as I say, DNA analysis facilitates our work greatly. However, it's not all powerful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Strinovic, you mentioned DNA analysis. On the list of people who were exhumed in the Ovcara mass grave, i.e., 200 people, 11 people have not been identified. They have been given a number, OCV 011, OCV 015. There are at least ten people who have not been identified. Since they have no name, I assume that families contacted the institute to try and find their relatives. Did you compare the DNA of these unidentified people with the hundreds or thousands of people that are looking for a relative to cross-reference the data and see whether, in terms of DNA analysis, identification is possible? How is it that today some people have been dug out of these mass graves and that these people still do not have a name?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the answer, for the record, there isn't 11 people not identified. I think there are seven people not identified in Ovcara in that report, because it says, the last page of the report, page 7, that up until the moment of writing this report, 193 bodies. Maybe it's a misunderstanding or misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a list which mentioned 11 bodies. Even if there are seven bodies, how is it that these persons have not been identified, particularly if there are relatives that are looking for them? A family that comes to see you, do you take a sample of their hair to be able to conduct a DNA analysis? I assume you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour, to be as brief and clear as possible. The problem of DNA identification precisely lies there, especially when we're talking about victims of war. We can't identify them. Now, we have the example of Ovcara, and as you said, there are 7 out of the 200 that we have not been able to identify. We started the process in 1996, and it's been 12 years since then, and we've been working on the matter intensively, but we still haven't identified seven persons. Now, why is that? At the Zagreb Cemetery, for example, we have 400 bodies that are not identified yet. They have been processed, but we have not ascertained who the people were, so a large number. We do have information about missing persons, and we have taken blood samples from most of these people, that is true, but unfortunately we still do not have all the relatives, all the blood samples, and here's why: Because some people moved out of the area, another portion has died, and in certain cases we don't know who the person is. And you asked about those seven specific cases. We don't know if they're on the list of 200 or 260 persons or whether there are some other people. For example, let me try and clarify this. We had a list for 260 missing persons, but there was no -- there were no women on that list, whereas in Ovcara we found the bodies of two women. So they weren't on the list but their bodies were found, and we managed to identify them. So these lists are not 100 per cent correct, especially in wartime. So you don't know who all the bodies are who are in a mass grave. We don't know who these seven are, whether they are people on the list or not. And, secondly, although every six months or one year we go out to look for relatives, ask them to give blood samples, and they come to us for assistance, but we still cannot solve all the cases in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On listening to you, I was thinking about those seven bodies that have not been identified. Can we assume the following? In the Ovcara mass grave, if victims had been buried a few days or a few months prior to that and that the persons who had been executed at Vukovar were then buried in the same place, with the forensic techniques you have, are you able to assess exactly on what date a body is buried or aren't you able to do that, which would explain why seven people from Ovcara may have come from the hospital who, to date, have not been identified yet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to answer that question, Your Honour. What I can say is this: There is no certain method today or procedure by which one would be able to determine, within the space of seven, ten or twelve years, when the people were killed, but what we can say, when we are faced with a mass grave of this kind, is that we can say that those -- the people in the grave were killed at around the same time. Now, just to illustrate how difficult it is, we determine the age of the body, that is to say, how long the body -- the person has been dead until the corpse was found on the basis of certain signs. There are no scientific methods by which you can do this, just signs to indicate that a body has laid there for a long time. So we established the signs of death, whether it has been skeletonised, whether it has -- whether saponification has taken place, what kind of putrifaction has taken place and so on. In Ovcara, where we have a large number of bodies, around 200, on the surface -- not because they have been killed previously, but because they are on the surface, those bodies had already been skeletonised or partially skeletonised, whereas bodies that were dug into the earth deeper and the last bodies that were found, those bodies were saponified, not because these people were killed later but because they were dug deeper into the ground, where the process of putrifaction, decay, was much slower and the process was different and saponification set in so that the deeper embedded bodies were saponified, whereas scar tissue was evident, skin was evident and so on, whereas the skeletonised bodies on the surface were killed on the same day or around the same time, but the bodies have a different appearance because they were on the surface and were rather skeletonised rather than saponified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Of course, we could spend hours on this, but one last question. What about these seven unidentified bodies? I suppose they have a DNA profile. I suppose that for each one of them, you conducted DNA tests. And for each one of these seven bodies, I suppose you have a DNA profile. It looks like a barcode that we're all familiar with .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. All these seven unidentified corpses, well, we isolated their DNA, their DNA, but we haven't got anything to compare it with and then have a DNA profile to match it up with the relatives. So we need blood samples in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, I would like now to turn your mind to the exhumation at Ovcara. You were involved in monitoring that exhumation; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When was the mass grave at Ovcara discovered?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The mass grave at Ovcara was discovered in October 1992, when Clyde Snow, an anthropologist from America, came to Ovcara, and he discovered a gravesite. And on the surface or just below the surface he came across human bones, and they were the bodily remains of a young male. And he found a cross that the person obviously had worn around his neck, and he established with a great deal of certainty that it was probably a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Concerning this work done by Dr. Snow, I want to show you some photos. Your Honours, it is the 65 ter number 2163. It is a Powerpoint presentation with 28 slides related to the initial discovery of the site. In your binders and the accused's binders, you find the slides at binder 7, document 42. I would ask that you see these photographs, Dr. Strinovic, and then comment on them. I will tell the usher when the slide should be stopped. So, Your Honour, the Powerpoint presentation will not work because all the computers are not working today, so we have these photos in e-court with one number. We can see the photo one by one, and I stop the photos. Of course, it will take a lot of time, but it's not [indiscernible]. So let's continue, let's go on. Go on. You can continue until slide 5. Yes, continue. Can you tell us -- can you comment on this photo you have seen, and in particular this one? What is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to say briefly that I was in this particular locality for the first time, that is to say, the mass grave at Ovcara, in 1996, and these are photographs taken earlier. So when I arrived there, I'd like to say that on the right-hand side it's a large field. On the left-hand side, we can see some trees, and along the edges of those trees there's an area right by that little wood there or -- is the site where the grave was. The photographs we saw earlier on, aerial photographs, there you can see the location of the mass grave or, rather, the first photograph taken by Clyde Snow linked to the skeleton that we saw. You could see the skull, in actual fact; obviously, a human skull. And that is what led to further investigation and suspicions that there was, indeed, a mass grave there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: We can continue with the next photo. Just stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know the person or the persons in this photos, the people here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I know one of them, Clyde Snow. He is the elderly gentleman wearing glasses and a hat, standing by this wire fence. When Clyde came for the first time in October 1992 to Ovcara, he asked for military assistance or, rather, that the area be secured, and it was secured as you see it with this barbed wire. And that's how the place was secured, as far as I know, right up to 1996, when the exhumation process began.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay, you can continue. Go on, go on, until I say, "Stop," please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I ought to mention the following: This site is the site of the mass grave, and you can see that water has been collected in the indentation, and that's where Clyde Scott [as interpreted] found the photo we saw in the slide a moment ago. That's a slight depression there where the water has gathered, and this on the very edge of the thicket or the trees. On the other side, you have the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay, let's continue. Go on. Continue. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is this in this photo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We can see part of a human body here, the arm, with part of the clothing, and this was the beginning of the deeper exhumation that took place in December 1992. It was a trial exhumation, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What's this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the trial exhumation, preliminary exhumation. There was very little time and the commission had to leave the area quickly for political reasons, so that they wanted to probe the area to see how many people might be buried, then how big the grave might be, so they made a probe and dug for some eight or nine metres and tried to establish what earth had been dug up and what soil was untouched, and so they deduced from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's continue. Go on. Let's continue. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you explain us what are doing -- what are these soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: These soldiers established some damage -- strange damage on the trees growing there, and that was right in the vicinity of the grave. They found some defects, holes running through the trees, which had obviously been caused by projectiles passing through the tree trunks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, were these Russian UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as I know, as of 1992, the guards securing the area were guards from the Russian Battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What is this in the photo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we were discussing a moment ago. This is a body buried on the surface, in the surface layer, and the soil had fallen away from the corpse. This is a male skull, skeletonised, as you can see, and it's about a year since this person died.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you see here? Let's move to the other slide that is more clear, the following.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is an object found on the person on the surface; that is to say, the skeletonised skull we saw a moment ago belongs to that particular person, and nearby was this rosary or pendant worn by young people, especially in the 1990s. It was a symbol of belonging to the Croatian people, being an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's continue. I think we can move very quickly to the end of the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What does this photo represent?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, we have the symbol of a saint esteemed by the Croatian people, and very often it was sewn onto the clothing worn by a Croat, a Croatian national.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think it is the last one, the last one photo. Okay. Dr. Strinovic, looking at those slides, briefly can you describe the process that occurred in that first excavation that you have already done and what did doctors know made after this discovery?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about Ovcara, let me repeat that Ovcara was discovered in October 1992 and then was visited in December by Clyde Snow and another team of experts, when they did the probes and trial exhumations, and this area was secured, as I said, by the Russian forces. It was cordoned off with barbed wire, and as far as I know the site remained intact, untouched, until the exhumation officially began in 1996, on the 30th of October, and went on until the 2nd of November, 1996, when anthropologists and archaeologists, international ones, conducted the full exhumation of the area. Would you like me to go into that in greater detail or shall we do that in due course about the actual exhumation process at Ovcara itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think maybe it's time for the break, Your Honour, and maybe we can continue this topic later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. You may proceed, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to tender the photos that we've seen into evidence. It's 65 ter number 2163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for the photos, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents shall be given Exhibit number P611. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, you say that the Commission for Detained and Missing Persons was set up in 1991. Did the Croatian commission and the Yugoslav commission meet at the time before the discovery of the mass grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, the commission started meeting in 1992 on a regular monthly basis, once a month, initially, and we met in Hungary, in Budapest, so -- or in another place, so we met before the -- before the discovery of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you discuss the problem of the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, one of the principal topics of our talks, at least from the Croatian side, was the question of the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital, so that every time -- I'm not sure of the number, but I believe we had between seven and eight meetings in 1991, and that was on the top of the agenda every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: And from the representative of the Yugoslav commission, at the time it was Yugoslav, after it became Serbian commission, what was the response to this issue? Did they have information in relation to these missing people?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It was really such a long time ago, I cannot recall all the details. But to the best of my recollection, we did not get any information in relation to Ovcara, nor was it recognised, acknowledged as such. But it was about some persons, but not about that particular case, so we never got that particular reply from them, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that the full exhumation of the site occurred in 1996; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was in the fall of 1996, from October to November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know why the site wasn't exhumed or the bodies weren't exhumed in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996? It took four or five years -- four years before exhuming these people, these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the international organisations were willing and prepared and had ready teams to start exhumations in 1992 and 1993, but due to political reasons, political considerations on the Serb side, that was prohibited so that no exhumations could take place until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Was that area Serbian territory until 1996?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It was the so-called Krajina, so that, yes, it was in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know that if between 1992 and 1996 the site that was found by Dr. Snow was protected? And by whom, if "yes," of course?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said, in October 1992 Dr. Snow found that gravesite, and at that time it was secured by barbed wire and it was guarded by Russian soldiers, by their units with international forces known as UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: When the site was discovered, were you or the people involved in this process, were you sure it was people missing from the hospital in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: According to what information we did receive, and the information would be gathered in Croatia immediately after the disappearance of a person or a group of persons, namely, the list would be immediately made within a matter of days, we did suspect that those people who went missing from the hospital and were seen at the Ovcara farm could be the persons at that locality who had perished, and we really did suspect that the Ovcara gravesite actually had the people from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you have an idea how many people were buried there in October 1992, when the site was discovered by Dr. Snow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What we knew was that -- that about 260 per cent had been taken from the Vukovar Hospital aboard five buses. And we did not know the exact number at the Ovcara gravesite, but we supposed that it was a large number and that it could have been the 260 persons who had gone missing from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the document 65 ter number 1697. It is in the binder 7, document 43, for the accused and for the assistance of Your Honours. It is a newspaper article dated 28th of October 1992 from Novi Vijesnik. It is the fourth document in your binder, Dr. Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. That article has not been disclosed in full, just in parts, and it was photocopied in a very odd way. The second question is the relevance of it. What does a newspaper article have to do with the exhumations and identifications of bodies carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you say, Mr. Ferrara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the copy of the entire article, the back, the other part of the article. I don't know what is missing. I think nothing is missing here. For the relevance, it is an article published immediately after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please give us the number? It's not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, 65 ter number 1697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is the number of the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. It is binder 7, document 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's binder 7, fourth document in that binder. 2289, that's the number I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: 43, yes. Your Honour, it's 43, document 43, but the 65 ter number with the document is what I said is 1697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, could you read the title of the article?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: You probably mean this title: "Any survivors in the darkness of Ovcara?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So it would be that after the discovery of the mass grave, it was possible there were still people alive, missing from Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that in relation to the list of the persons missing from the Vukovar Hospital, some people were later found alive. Those are people who perhaps were released during transportation to the Ovcara farm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, please take a look at my copy of that article. On one side, you have the cover page of the newspaper -- of the newspaper page. On the other page, you have the other part. You don't have the middle. In other words, the photocopying of it was not done properly. That is why this cannot be used as a document, not to mention the objection regarding the relevance of this text. Such as it stands, it cannot be used. This is not a complete text. Maybe you have it in the English version. I do not have it in the Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have the complete text, but what is interesting is that on the 28th of October, 1992, there was an article raising the issue of whether there were survivors from Ovcara. That's the issue. Now, as to the article, that's secondary. Please proceed, Mr. Ferrara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Exactly what you said. So I would like to tender this document into evidence. I mean only the title of the article, not the content, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title. Very well. Let's have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this comment of yours can also refer to the question: Were there any discussions in the public about whether there were any people who survived from among those who were taken away from the hospital? But in order for this article to be exhibited, it has to be complete. It is not complete in the Serbian language, apart from the fact of its -- the fact that it's not really relevant. But I cannot use it in my counter-examination if it is not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give it an MFI number, Mr. Registrar, because apparently it's not complete.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is going to be given MFI number P612. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: My case manager has already requested a better copy of the article. I think we can provide it before the end of the examination of Dr. Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, did you have the opportunity to read the report of a preliminary site exploration of a mass grave near Vukovar in the former Yugoslavia drafted by Physicians for Human Rights? It is 65 ter number 1773. It is in the binder 1, document 4.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have the opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you briefly summarise what did emerge from this preliminary report that was drafted in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in brief, I can say that this text speaks about the existence of a mass grave, about what was done at that time, that is, in 1992, and how it was secured, the gravesite. Just general things associated with the location of that gravesite, with the Ovcara locality, and an attempt at carrying out further exhumations, which however was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that you went to Ovcara in 1996, when the exhumation started. When you went there in 1996, was the situation similar to the one described in this report or did you notice any relevant change after four years, about three years and a half?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I could answer in this way: I was not there in 1992 and 1993, but according to the photographs, i.e., the description that we are talking about now, the situation has not considerably changed. The only thing which has changed is the vegetation that has grown, so that that has changed it, but basically it is the same place as it was. It is the same since 1992, when Clyde Snow found the gravesite, until 1996, when we went there to attend the scene and watch the exhumations being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question beforehand. You can guess that I examined -- I scrutinised with great care this report by American physicians based in Boston, and upon reading the report, one notices that they probably had information from witnesses. That's page 2, where they said that according to some witnesses, some reservists, JNA soldiers and officers, and then all the events are described at 6.00 and so on. So all that is very specific, so obviously they had information. Obviously. So when did you hear of the existence of this report, which was done on the 18th of January, 1993? You, when did you read it? Because it is a very detailed and very precise report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw it for the first time yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see. You'd never -- so you found out about its existence yesterday only; you had no knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And this is a very detailed report in which they explain that there was a bulldozer that dug a grave of nine metres by seven, so everything was said in this report. Obviously, they must have had information. And I was somewhat surprised, I must confess, when the doctor that went there found a skull, I mean, they must have had information, prior information. You can't just, by happenstance, find a skull sort of out of the soil. I mean, there was fighting everywhere, of course, but how could you imagine that beneath that skull there were 200 bodies? They must have had information, had they not? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say what I said before. We knew that about 260 persons had been taken from the Vukovar Hospital by buses in that direction, and we got information that they were at the farm at Ovcara. After that, all trace was lost of them. On the basis of that information, we could suspect that those bodies would be somewhere in the vicinity. That is how I drew that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Let's have a number for the document, very official document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P613. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, you say the full exhumation occurred in 1996. Who conducted that exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, these were experts designated by the ICTY. They were international experts from all over the world. I do not know the exact name of the commission which carried out the exhumation and the subsequent processing, but as far as I know, these were experts appointed by the ICTY and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was it conducted under the Yugoslav Tribunal authority or was it in any way involved with the Yugoslav Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, when the Ovcara exhumation started, there were present as monitors representatives of Croatia, which is to say myself and some other people, and representing Serbia was a professor from Nis. And as far as I can remember, there was a doctor from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How long did the exhumation last of retrieving the bodies from the grave and delivering them? Approximately, of course.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The exhumation started on the 30th of August, 1996, and lasted until the 2nd of October, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where were the bodies transferred -- transported after the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When the bodies were taken out, they would be placed in white bags, and all together were then transported to the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zagreb at Salata. At that time, there was constructed a special space precisely for that purpose, for the identification of the Ovcara victims, and later those premises were used for all subsequent identifications that were conducted at our institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Where were the autopsies conducted, and when, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies would be transported to Zagreb, to the Forensic Medical Institute, into special rooms tailormade for that particular purpose, which are today still used for that particular purpose, the processing of victims of war. They are some 50 metres away from our own premises, those of the Pathology Institute. This was done also by international experts, just as the exhumation itself. There were monitors present as well from all over Yugoslavia, including from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So in relation to this first phase, the exhumation and autopsy, your role as the forensic pathologist within the commission, as we say, was to -- only to monitor rather than conduct the exhumation; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: After the -- and after the autopsies were completed, who was in charge for identification of the body? Who was put in charge?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: After all the mortal remains had been completely processed, they started on the 5th of October and were finished on the 16th of November, 1996, of all mortal remains of the persons found at Ovcara, protocols were written for some time after that, the administrative part of the procedure, that is. After that, the mortal remains were handed over to the Croatian authorities, i.e., to the Forensic Medicine Institute, in other words to me, who was in charge of the identification team. The moment we received the mortal remains, we also received the autopsy reports, reports which contained descriptions of the bodies with all the details associated with their identification. But at that time, we were not given the causes of death in respect of the persons concerned. That was omitted from the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why not? Why were not you given the causes of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The explanation which was given to us was that what we had received was sufficient for us for identification purposes and that the cause of death was a bit of information which is of relevance to the Court and would be submitted to the ICTY, rather than to us in charge of identification stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Before moving to the identification process, that is, the process that you were personally involved with as a member of the commission and as a forensic expert, I would like to show you a serious of photographs taken from the exhumation that occurred in 1996. Please, can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 2710. It's a serious of 35 photos taken during the exhumation. As before, I will stop you, the usher, when we have some photos that we need a comment from the witness, from the expert. Is in the binder 6, document 25, Your Honours, for your assistance and the accused. Can you explain, Dr. Strinovic, what we see in this photo number 1? Was this fence erected we see on the right side of the photo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the locality of the mass grave which is in the middle of this space. We see some trees on the left side and a fence on the right-hand side which was erected in order to divide the mass gravesite from the rest of the area. Then tents were erected to house the people in charge of the exhumation itself. So this fence was put up in order to divide the area of the mass gravesite from the other area where people were moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's turn to photograph 2, the second photo in the series. Doctor, we see a white building - it's not very clear - on the right side of the photo. Can you tell us, what is this white building?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: These are tents that were pitched on the other side of the fence which separates the mass grave from the rest of the terrain, so this is where the people who did the exhumations were, where they rested, where they waited for their scheduled exhumation times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: If we can slowly click through photos from 3 to 4 and stop at photograph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Doctor, looking at photograph 5, what do we see here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the access to the gravesite at Ovcara. A road was subsequently cleared to enable machines and people to arrive at the site. We can also see the fence which separates the gravesite from the outer world.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Again, if we could move through the photos until photo 10, photograph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the purpose of all these photos, Mr. Ferrara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's to show the situation at Ovcara that was found in 1996 and how the situation was exactly the same as 1992, so it was not any kind of interfering on this site in these four years. It was protected. And also we see the body situation, how the bodies were found, and the skulls, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is this a disputed question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think everything is disputed by the accused. If it's not disputed, we can tender the photo even without showing it, because, you see, we filed a motion to take judicial notice of this fact -- sorry, as adjudicated facts, and until today the accused has challenged this motion, so I think that really everything is disputed. We can ask the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You see, my point is that I would be hesitant even to admit them into evidence because I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think it's relevant, of course. Maybe when we finish seeing the photos --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, how many photos did you want to show us, how many more?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the photos in total are 35, but I will stop only on some of them. Of course, it's a bunch of photos all together. So if we can move to photo 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: A trench that was excavated can be seen to establish the boundaries of the gravesite. This is the way we dig in order to reach a boundary without damaging the bodies, but in order to determine the size of the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What was the size of the grave; do you remember? Approximately, of course.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It is hard for me to give you the exact dimensions. I believe that they were of the order of nine times seven metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's move to photo 12. Can you tell us, looking at this plastic sheeting, what's the purpose of this plastic sheeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, in 1993 and in 1992, when we did the trial excavations, a part of the grave was protected in this way and that plastic foil was then covered by earth, by soil. That is why it remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue, please, to photo 14 -- or 15, sorry. Is this 14 or 15? We see here an excavator that we see in this photograph. How did that assist the excavation, the excavator ?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
