utterances.text: Well, I can tell you this: In most cases, there were large gravesites, a large surface area, and these were small excavators, earth-moving material, and they were of great assistance, because in digging the trenches the size of a grave would save time. Now, of course, when the excavator came upon a body, they would stop using the excavator and go on to manually digging up the grave. In large gravesites, in most cases, especially if they are at great depths like two or three metres, then of course digging up the bodies is much quicker if you have these excavators to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: If we can move to the slide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time has been used so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: If we can go to slide 23. It's not this one, it's not this one. Next one, please. It's not this. 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Doctor, can you explain what you see here and indicate what the meaning of that number 5?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The photographs are rather dark, but that's how it was in the actual locality. Here we can see a number of bodies intermingled, and the number 5 means that the individual who will be taken out is the fifth person in order. This was on the surface, and every body was given a number. It said "Ovcara," numbers 1 to 200. This is obviously body number 5 extracted from the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you have 20 minutes left, so please show us the important photograph which you wish to tender into evidence, and please go to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: This was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So you said that numbers were assigned to the bodies that were in the grave, and this number followed the body until now? So until now, this is the body of Ovcara victim number 5; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have an exhibit number for the photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These other documents shall be given Exhibit number P614. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: If we can go now to the 65 ter document 2689. It is a table entitled "Paragraph 49." It relates to a chart that is attached to your report, prepared for the Milosevic case. So it's binder 6, document 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you comment on the statistics in this table?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The table shows the 200 bodies, of which we show the number that -- the number of people suffering gunshot wounds, trauma and so on. Of the 200 individuals who were killed, 195 were killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, 188 were gunshot wounds, six individuals were killed through trauma, and one person was killed by stabbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What does it mean, "killed by trauma," "killed by shooting," "killed by stabbing," "trauma"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Most of these individuals found in Ovcara were killed by gunshot wounds; that is, projectiles fired from firearms. The people that died through trauma, that means that we cannot determine the means used to kill them. It must have been blows with certain objects which led to injury and death, other than firearms. Whereas stab wounds, since the tissue was preserved, we were able to ascertain that there were a number of stab wounds in the torso and neck of the individual concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What is this -- when you say "stabbing," I don't see the word "stabbing" here. Where do you find this "stabbing"; under the category "Other Violence," maybe in there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the column where the cause of death has been ascertained. Under "Other," other violent deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the youngest age and the eldest age of the people found killed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. As you can see in paragraph 49 of my report -- [interpretation] The youngest was 16. The oldest was 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this table into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have an exhibit number for this table, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be Exhibit number P615. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have the document 65 ter number 2687. It is in binder 6, document 28. It is the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is it this list represent, and who prepared this -- drafted this list? It is the document 10 in your binder, 10.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On this table, we can see the names -- the first names and last names of the persons identified at Ovcara, their date of birth, and it says "Pos ID," that is to say, positive identification as a separate column under "Status." So it is a list of persons from Ovcara, along with their dates of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be Exhibit number P616. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we don't have enough time to examine with the expert, of course, the autopsy report. I will put questions to the expert in relation to just three of these autopsy report. In relation to one autopsy report, my aim is adding a general explanation of the standard template followed in drafting all the autopsy report, and in fact you can see that all the report are drafted according to the same template. And I think that the answers given by the expert concerning one report can fit exactly to all of them that I will ask to tender into evidence. In addition, I want the doctor to comment specific details in other two autopsy report, because they are particularly interesting for our case. It's one of the women that was killed at Ovcara and one of the stabbing that we found in these bodies. To tender the autopsy report, I prepared a list. I have here a hard copy for Your Honours and for the accused as well, where I mentioned all the -- the number of the autopsy with this reference the doctor gave us is OCV 001, 002 and so on, with identification, so with the name of the -- of the body, of the person who was found there, the date of birth, the date of the document, the autopsy, the English ERN, the 65 ter in our list, and the identification document, if it exists, because in a lot of bodies, as the expert will explain, were found a lot of document, identification document or other documents that were used to identify the person found in the mass grave, and the photos were taken. Of course, I did not prepare the set of photos related to all victims. I selected only 10 of them, just to give an explanation to the Trial Chamber. So if we can give this list, and I want to comment the -- from the witness that 65 ter number 2297, that is the autopsy report in relation to Ovcara victim number 9, Josip Balog.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what binder is the autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's binder 2, document 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, if you can, very briefly, of course: Is this the autopsy report that was prepared by the international group -- the international group of pathologists; I'm right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. More or less the 200 reports were done in this way, like the one we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you comment on the main entries of this report? Of course, we don't want you to read, but just that short area.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the essential points with respect to the report and the prototype, you always have the number of Ovcara, Ovcara 9, then the date when the autopsy was conducted, and brief information regarding the age, sex and whether they were left-handed or right-handed. Then any interesting pieces of clothing are listed and other facts that might be of interest for identification purposes, personal documents, if they are of interest. In this specific case, what was found was an ID card made out to Josip Balog, which means that identification was made easier. Then there's an external examination with descriptions of what was found on the bodies. Some were skeletonised, others were well preserved, which made the description much more detailed. The state of the skin, various deformities that the person was born with or gained later on in life. And if the organs were present, then a description of those organs; an examination of the teeth and their description, which are especially important for identification purposes. Then there was a column specific to Ovcara which was any signs of hospital treatment, because it was thought that most of these people had been treated in hospital, they had been patients in a hospital. Then traumas linked and associated with death, and the injuries that were found, if any evidence such as projectiles or anything else that were found that could have been the cause of death, those are recorded. And then you have the column "Cause of death" and "Manner of death," "Killing."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: You say that you did not receive the entire report until such time, I don't remember. Which part of this report did you receive from the internationals?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, when we received the bodies, we received a partial report from the international experts which went up to "Trauma associated with death." We didn't receive that column, "Trauma associated with death," neither did we receive the column "Cause of death."

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this report into evidence, together with the other 199 that are indicated in my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2297 shall be given Exhibit number P617. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the other document, I think the exhibit number will be assigned outside the court, not in court, because we need one hour to [indiscernible] the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is document 2856; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I was not very clear in my explanation. The document 2856, we have to show -- we have to show to the witness this 2856. This is a table for your assistance to follow the document in the court binder, the autopsy report. Now I show to the witness this document 2856. That is the document that was admitted already in the Mrksic and Milosevic. But in this document I gave you, it is more complete because we found the number of identification document and the photos document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So show him the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the document 2856. Your Honours, this chart that we prepared, it is only a list of 200 autopsy report. Of course, I have yet to enter the autopsy report, but if you want, I can tender all of them, but I think it is not necessary. We can tender only the list, and we can have the exhibit number outside the court. So we can have an exhibit number starting from the chart, one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you have two alternatives. You can ask to tender all the autopsy reports or you are just asking for this document to be tendered into evidence and that refers to all the autopsy reports. It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender all the autopsy reports, but to have a quick list -- short list of the autopsy report, I created this chart. Of course, I have the autopsy report here with me, but I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give a number to the list, but show the table to the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: 2856 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: It is document 12, your document 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what does this chart represent?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This table represents the names and surnames of persons who have been identified and the way in which they were identified, which means that it was the classical method that was applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I think you're -- 12.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 12. On this table, we have the names and surnames of the persons identified, their date of birth, who conducted the autopsy, when the autopsy was carried out, and in what way; the classical method or in any other way. The date of birth of the individual that was identified is also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do we have in this chart the reference to the autopsy report, so the number of the autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is the number Ovcara 1. Yes, the number's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So we have all the autopsy report number until 200, or we see 200; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an exhibit number for this document, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be given Exhibit number P618. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Just in relation to the victim that we have seen before, Mr. Josip Balog, can we have very quickly the 65 ter number 2706 in the screen. It are the photos taken of the body. If we can move very quickly to the photo. Your Honours, these are a set of photos taken of this victim number 9, that is Josip Balog, in this case. These is just a template of the photo that were taken of the body, and I'd like to tender just ten of them that are in our 65 ter list, just as an example of the video was taken in -- was made in the pit. So if we can go to most interesting, to the photo 17, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, do you feel that these photographs are really necessary or not, since we have the list that refers to all the autopsy reports? Do we really need to have these photographs, do you think? Technically speaking, it's not a problem as far as I'm concerned, but do we really need these photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tender just this set of photographs for one victim, just to have an idea of what activity it was made in the field. I think it's important, because, for example, with this victim we found we have the paper document, the identification paper at the photo 18, so the doctor has explained a lot of times we found these kind of documents in the victims, which is easier to identify them. So if you go there, the doctor can confirm in the photo 18. I think it's important also because we have this list of people missing from the hospital and the people that was found in the pit on the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to gain some time: When the bodies were exhumed, you found ID papers, for instance, on some of the bodies, in the case of Josip Balog, you found this document during the exhumation. Coins were found, money was found, and various documents were found. Can you confirm that all of this was found on the bodies during the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, I can tell you what was found. In some cases it was personal documents, in others it was medical documents or something similar that indicated the identity of the individual, and all this helped in the identification process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when it says in the column "Classical identification," it is thanks to this that the body has been identified, all the more so that this document was found on the body; is this why this is termed classical form of identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the only method of identification. We cannot give a name and surname to a person only on the basis of a document. We must find other elements, too, regarding height, sex, and various other elements that bear out and ascertain the identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give an exhibit number to all these photographs. Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these photographs shall be given Exhibit number P619. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 2371. That is in the binder 4, document 25. It is 16 in your binder. It is the autopsy report of Ovcara victim 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the cause of death for this victim?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In the case of Ovcara 174, it was multiple stabbing wounds to the torso, head and neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that the only lethal wounds in this case was a stabbing; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I seek to tender these documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be given Exhibit number P620. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 2503. It is the Ovcara victim number 095. This is one of the two women found at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this victim?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, this is a female. She was killed with multiple gunshot wounds to the head, and upper leg, the pelvis area, and also the thorax, the ribs, et cetera. So there were gunshot wounds all over her body, from the neck down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Would it be possible to say -- it is to say that she was pregnant or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the basis of the autopsy report and what was found during the autopsy, there was no conclusions made as to whether she was pregnant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Why not? Can you explain us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The reason is that due to putrifaction, the fetus, which is composed of water mostly, disintegrates and disappears, and therefore pregnancy in cases of this kind, that is to say, persons who were buried in the ground for a long time after death, no traces of pregnancy are found or of the fetus are found.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be Exhibit P621. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Let's move to the other location. It's Vocin, and I have really a few questions on the location. Please can we have on the screen the 65 ter number 2670.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Vocin is a location where the pattern of the joint criminal enterprise is supposed to be shown, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vocin relates to deliberate conduct, deliberate. Are you saying that in Vocin, people were killed? Is that what you would like to say? Vocin is part of the deliberate pattern. Are you wanting to establish that people were killed in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the Vocin crime scene in relation to your finding? Were you there? Did you go to Vocin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the information we had, the people had been killed in Vocin on the 13th of November, 1992, and the autopsy was done on the 17th of December. It was carried out in Slatina, which is a place in the vicinity of Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: How many corpse were found there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Forty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender into evidence this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be given Exhibit number P622. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Did you take part to the identification process of the bodies found at this mass grave in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In Vocin, it was not a classical mass grave, but rather when the dead bodies were found in the street, in the houses, they were collected and taken there. This was a village where these bodies were found. As I say, they were of 43 persons, so they were well preserved, so that the autopsy was performed just as in a situation when you deal with recently deceased persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, then, document 834. The document is already admitted into evidence, Your Honours, as P581. I want to ask the witness only if this is the list of the victims found at Vocin. It is the list in binder 7, document 46, the 21st of your binder, 21.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is that list, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen the photo with 65 ter number 2715.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: This photo and the following -- the next one is related to a victim Stojan Nenadovic. Dr. Strinovic, what detail -- what does this photo tell us about the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is an elderly man who died a violent death due to multiple blows by a blunt object to his body. We can see on his shoulder and right arm irregular traces which are consistent with the blows of a chain or a similar object, and irregular trauma on the head which could have been inflicted by a booted foot, by a hand, fist, or some other similar object.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Do you know why this person was killed? And if you know, how did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Slatina to conduct the autopsy, we were informed by the police guarding the area that it was a male of Serb ethnicity whose son had been a member of the Croatian Army, and that is why this man was killed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: So is this the only --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This exceeds the possibilities of the expert report. The expert is here speaking about the motives -- the possible motives of the killing. He can just say one thing, which is that the victim was identified and that it was a Serb. Why the person had been killed, that is beyond the expert's -- the witness's capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you did, as I did, participate in an autopsy, you would know that the forensic pathologist carrying it out seeks information from the people bringing the body as to the circumstances. So before he starts with the medical examination as to the manner of death, that's what you do, isn't it, Doctor? You are brought a corpse, and then you ask questions to find out in which circumstances the person was found, met her end, and maybe fell out of a window, was run over by a bus. That's what is asked before you carry out the post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is exactly how we proceed with every forensic medical autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender into evidence this photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give us a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be Exhibit number P623. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: My last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Concerning these 43 people killed at Vocin, did you have the opportunity to review the expert report containing the forensic analysis of bodily injuries and corporal wounds of victims from Vocin drafted by Dr. Kraus, Zorislav? That is 65 ter number 1748. That is for your assistance, Your Honours, and the accused, in the binder 2, document 25.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to read that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, really briefly, the content of this report and if you agree with the conclusion in this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kraus, on the basis of the records made by forensic medicine physicians in Zagreb, us who conducted the procedure, he formed an opinion -- drafted an opinion for the needs of the Court. On the basis of our records, he established the causes of death, which we had also established. He established the manner of the infliction of the wounds and possibly the position of the person inflicting the wound and the person who died. All this was derived from our own protocol which we had written and submitted to the Court, and I fully subscribe to those findings, to that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be P624. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before ending the questions, I ask to tender into evidence the report of Dr. Strinovic bearing 65 ter number 7250, drafted for this case, and his previous report with 65 ter number 2672, drafted for the Milosevic and Mrksic case that we used today for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give two MFI numbers. Indeed, only after the cross-examination will we decide whether we need to give final numbers or not. So we need to have MFI numbers for 7250 and 2672.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these two documents shall be given MFI numbers P609 and P610. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, and concerning the document that was tendered, the press article that received the MFI P612, here I have a better copy of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give the copy to Mr. Seselj so that he can check that it is now a complete document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you now have the complete article. Let's give a number. So the MFI number will become now a final number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI document P612 will become Exhibit P612. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to break for 20 minutes, and then Mr. Seselj can start with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you now have the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, when was it that you were at this mass grave near Ovcara for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was in 1996, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember what month it was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1996, when I was at the mass grave, it was just before the excavations; that is, it was August or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did there exist this filled road, this road that you just showed us moments ago in the photograph, or was it constructed later?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Work was being done on the road about that time, but when it was finished, it is hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Otherwise, one could not reach the mass grave in a regular car; one had to use an all-terrain vehicle or a tractor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's the way it was. It was a very impassable road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was actually the field road used by tractors, combine, harvesters and such?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were there in August, that is the height of summer, that is the dry season, there is no rain; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it usually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In October and November, the rains are heavy and everything is soaked, so one cannot get there except by tractor or a caterpillar fitted vehicle or something similar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a specially for that purpose outfitted vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Strinovic. This answer of yours to this question is very important, although you may find it odd, because you know we had some false witnesses here who claimed that they used a private luxury car in November to reach from Ovcara to this pit to execute people. That is why I'm asking this, so that you don't think that my questions make no sense.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You supervised, oversaw the exhumations as director of the Forensic Medicine Institute in the majority of cases; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally, not only in this case. Rather, I organised the work but the supervising of the exhumations was done by other people, but I was there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This included exhumations where the Serbs had been victims, like in Pakracka Poljana and Gospic, victims of mass crimes, that is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me one thing. When you saw this number, 260 found bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're both speaking the same language. So, Witness, before answering questions put to you by Mr. Seselj, wait for a little bit to allow the interpreters to translate what you have said, because you're talking very fast and the interpreters have difficulty following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This mass grave at Ovcara, I suppose, is the biggest in terms of the number of exhumed bodies. Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In Croatia, that is the largest mass grave that has been detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when you saw this number of 260 bodies, did it seem a bit odd? 200 executed people could not have been the result of some spontaneous action by a gang on the rampage or some territorial seeking revenge, or any other groups. Was it not obvious that someone had ordered the execution of precisely 200 people, because it is a very small degree of probability that it was precisely 200 people that were killed and thrown into a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you this in answering: I really never gave any thought to what you're asking me now. I was there as an expert. I came to the mass grave, I heard what the number was. Why precisely 200, I cannot really say. It is very difficult for me to give you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I see in the case of the murder of Stojan Nenadovic, the Serb, you ventured into some -- to give some lengthier explanations of these secondary circumstances which had led to the crime. The Croatian public was informed about this case of Ovcara very much, there was very much written about it; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct. Victims of Ovcara are, unfortunately, one of the sad symbols of Croatia, and very much was indeed written and said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then you should be aware of the fact that not all the prisoners who had been taken to Ovcara had been killed. 207 actually came there, but 7 were released, their lives were spared. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I know that not all the people who had been taken to the farm of Ovcara were executed. Some were let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A total of seven were set free. We know some of them, Dragutin Berghofer, Emil Cakalic, Vilim Karlovic and some others. I cannot recall all the names, but we have established with certainty that there have been seven of them. As an expert of forensic medicine, as a secondary circumstance you found 200 bodies. You know that there had been 207 prisoners, and someone decided to let 7 go. So someone had planned that precisely 200 be executed, and those who carried out the order wouldn't do anything more than they had been ordered to. A crime is a crime, there is no doubt about it, but those who committed the crime did not want to surpass the figure of 200; isn't that obvious?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Look, I cannot give you an answer to the question the way you put it. I know about these seven people who were released. There was a story associated with each one of them as to why he or -- he had been released, either knew a Serb soldier or was on good terms with somebody. So there was a reason why these seven people were set free. As to this precise number of 200, I cannot give you an answer, either as an expert or I in my personal capacity, why it had been that precise number. Was it accidentally or purposefully, I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We had occasion here to see that some other people also tried to save their acquaintances or friends, and once the number of seven had been filled, they were no longer able to do that. This doesn't say anything to you, does it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have given you an answer to that. I don't know about that. I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know that there was a larger number of people at Ovcara, that a large number of people had been at Ovcara, and a large number of people participated in the executions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the number of people who participated in the executions or those who were at Ovcara, I don't have that data. I couldn't tell you with precision or even approximately how many people were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you should know how many pieces of weaponry were used in the execution, because you established that on the basis of a review of the found bullets or cartridges; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can give you an answer to this question by saying that I know how many people were killed and what the wounds were which caused their deaths, but as regards the number of cartridges, that is up to the ballistic experts, those who looked for and found those bullets or cartridges, and this is a question for that kind of a specialist, for the ballistic expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in the course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following the question put to you by Mr. Seselj, let me now deal with a very technical issue. You, yourself, as part of your specialty, when you perform a post-mortem examination, do you have any ballistic data at your disposal, and don't you work in cooperation with the ballistics specialists in order for you, at the time of the autopsy, to be able to determine the path and the trajectory of bullets with the help of the ballistics expert by knowing, for example, what was the calibre of the weapon, what sort of impact that calibre can have? In other words, do you work in close cooperation with a ballistics expert or not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two stages. The first stage is when the autopsy is being carried out, when we look for the cause of death. When there is a gunshot wound, we can only sometimes determine the calibre with which the wound had been inflicted. If it involves those parts of the body, it is usually a bone where there is the exact diametre of the damage, which indicates what the calibre diametre -- the diametre of the calibre had been. So when we do the post-mortem, actually, we do not yet know what kind of a weapon was used. Later, when there is -- when the expert analysis for a court is being made in the second stage, we cooperate and form a joint opinion with a ballistic expert, and a ballistic expert determines the calibre of the projectile, its velocity and its characteristics, but not on the basis of the post-mortem report, because that is impossible, but on the basis of the found projectile which can be found in-situ, which is much more simpler, or in the body, rather, or if it is found elsewhere, which is a bit more complicated. So these expert analyses establish the characteristics of the projectile, whereas we establish the cause of death and the wound caused by projectile, but we cannot exactly say what kind of a projectile. We can draw indirect conclusions when there is vast damage, for instance, to the cranium or to the body, to the trunk, that speedy projectiles had been in question, those fired from a weapon used for war purposes. These are usually long-barrelled weapons which cause massive damage, which suggests to us that it was a high-speed projectile which could have been off this or that calibre, approximately. But the actual calibre is established by the ballistic experts by finding the projectile near or inside the body, or the cartridges of the projectile. We can seldom speak about the direction which the projectile took in passing through the body. We can talk about the direction from which the shot had been fired, but not the actual movement direction of the projectile in the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have seen a number of autopsy reports, and I was very surprised to see that at no point was there mention of whether the fire was opened at close range or not, because in cases of execution, you can very well imagine that this would be done very near to the victims. Did you also notice that in the reports, that none of that type of information was provided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that this information was missing, but I have to explain, as a forensic medical expert, why that is so. When wounds of this kind are in question, sometimes we can indeed establish that the shooting took place at close range or at a very short range of several millimetres from the body, in which case a massive, irregular defect will be caused by the shot, usually in the skull, where we can see great damage, massive damage of the bones, or in other parts of the body with massive damage to the tissue. Sometimes only the bones remain and we cannot see these characteristics, the close-range characteristics. But when we have a speedy projectile, there will be massive destruction, just as in the case of close range. And if we only have a bone and not soft tissue, it is difficult to tell what the distance had been. In other words, when we have bodies that have been in the earth for many years and the post-mortem is then done, and the distance of the shooting established, it is very hard to do on the basis of the remaining bones or tissue. But to establish that there had been a firing from close range, that is -- that is something that should have been described. I have no other explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you, Professor Strinovic. Was it possible to establish whether the individuals found in that mass grave were, for some of them, killed on the spot, after which they fell into the grave, or was it possible to establish whether some of them were killed in another location and whether their bodies were then removed and thrown into the mass grave once they had been executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can give you the following answer to that question: When you have gunshot wounds, which was the case in the majority of cases, multiple gunshot wounds had been in question, and death was a consequence of those gunshot wounds, obviously, where exactly the shooting had taken place is impossible to conclude on the basis of the wounds themselves. However, when the supplementary processing was conducted by ballistic experts, and we participated by just attending the scene, and they showed us the places where there were a large number of cartridges and were able to see vegetation, i.e., damage to vegetation, which indicates that there had been firing at that location, it was obvious that it was the site of the shooting. So most probably the bodies then fell into the already-dug pit. So I can just conclude by the indications, because the found cartridges and the damage to the trees on the other side, that it had been the place where the shooting had taken place. And as I said, most probably because of the multiple gunshot wounds, we can conclude that the shooting took place where the mass grave is, but we cannot say that with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, I presume that you know what a magnum revolver is.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It has a very specific calibre. Do you know what that calibre is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know, being no ballistic expert myself, but I know it has a very strong impact and effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As I have to be a ballistic expert, I know that it is a .357 calibre. It is called a magnum .357 calibre in ballistics. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It has a very specific calibre, and had that calibre was used in liquidating the prisoners, that cartridge would have had to be found; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It depends what part of the body was pierced, where the bullet passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A witness here claimed that one of the perpetrators, as criminals say, verified the people. I suppose that's the term they also use where you come from; namely, after the people had been executed, he came up to every victim and shot him in the head in order to finish him off. So if that were true, if that had been true, all the .357-calibre bullets would have been fired into the cranium, and that would have had to be established by the post-mortem analysis if that had really happened, really?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would have to have been seen by a post-mortem examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If there had been ten or so or more such cases, some of the bullets would have been fired into that part of the skull which certainly would not have been hit had the man been erect when he was executed and when he was being shot at. There is a part of the cranium, the top of the cranium, where you can shoot a man who is standing upright only from the air?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. If one bows his head, that part of the cranium is also exposed. If a man is standing, you can bend your head, so one can also shoot at the nape or at the top of the head if a man is in that position even standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you were testifying in the Belgrade case, the trial of the accused for the concrete crimes committed at Ovcara, you testified together with Dr. Milovan Kubat. He's a colleague of yours from Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was a colleague, a specialist for DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, as I'm no expert on that, and when I passed my examination in forensic medicine we had no DNA analysis, but I do remember my genetics from the third grade of high school, we call it "DNA," deoxyribonucleic acid. Why are you saying "DNA"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We have two ways of marking the same thing, basically. Actually, a part of Europe and America call it DNA, and some call it DNK, which is the same -- one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This deoxyribonucleic acid is what we're talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The third witness was professor Dr. Milos Tasic. You know him as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with the microphone, and instead of listening to Mr. Strinovic, I'm hearing the English interpretation. And you know how I abhor that language. I became depressed straight away and quite nervous and upset. So could that matter be put right, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. We're going to check what's going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's all right now. I can see -- I can hear the Serbian interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, the three of you, to all intents and purposes, tabled the report together. You went first, then Dr. Milovan Kubat and then Dr. Milos Tasic; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was. First of all, it was Kubat and I who provided identification with respect to identification at Ovcara, and when we had done our job, Professor Otasevic went in to present his opinion but we had already left, gone out, and we didn't hear his findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I assume you know what his findings were.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: While we were in the courtroom, we didn't take part, nor were we aware of his findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And two other Serbian specialists, forensic experts, took part in the post-mortem examinations, the autopsies conducted in Zagreb; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of them was Dr. Dobricanin; right? I'm not sure that I remember all their names, but do you remember who the doctors were?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Otasevic from Nis, he was together with me as a monitor during the autopsy conducted in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Otasevic, and there was another one, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not in Zagreb, but at Ovcara during the exhumation process, there was somebody from Vukovar. I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dr. Milos Tasic claimed that one can exclude the fact that gunshot wounds used in rifles was used for the liquidation of these victims. Do you agree with that? Or, rather, shots.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to give a decisive answer. I'd have to look through all the autopsy reports and the causes of death and descriptions, but I think that's the right answer. I don't think there's any dilemma. Pellets from shotguns, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I looked at all your 200 autopsies, and I never saw the mention of buckshot and pellets from buckshot. I'm quite certain of that. Now, if the Prosecutor considers otherwise, he can say so, but there's no mention of buckshot or pellets from buckshot.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's quite true. I don't remember any pellets being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which excludes the use of hunting rifles in this liquidation process?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it excludes the use of pellets, gunshot pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to Dr. Milos Tasic, 540 projectiles were found in the various bodies, and about 1.500 cartridges were found next to that mass grave. Are you aware of those facts and findings?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figures, but roughly those are the figures that I would say were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And all those cartridges and projectiles testify to the fact that Kalashnikov-type rifles were used, or pistol ammunitions from automatic pistols of the Skorpion type, and some other automatic pistols such as Hecklers or the M-56 type automatic rifles? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my answer would be the same as the previous one. I don't know for sure and precisely, but as far as I know, yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But mostly, we're dealing with bullets fired from Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the vast majority they were Kalashnikov bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You ascertained, and I assume that that is your most reliable piece of information, that of a total of 200 persons liquidated at Ovcara, that 6 were -- their death was caused by traumas and 1 by stab wounds inflicted to the body and neck; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. Those were our conclusions on the basis of the information received about the cause of death from the international experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there's no doubt that all the rest were killed through gunshot wounds, that is to say, through firearms?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From your report, I see that some of the bodies have more gunshot wounds, others were killed with just one bullet, but they were all killed from firearms. Now, when it comes to these six individuals who died as a result of trauma, you had certain methodology that you applied to ascertain those traumas, whether it was fracture to the skull, bone fractures, or anything similar; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when trauma was the cause of death, then quite obviously it was as a result of some blunt object inflicting a blow on the part of the body or head, leading to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that blunt object can be a rifle-butt; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, a blunt object; a rifle-butt or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A metal pipe, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a metal pipe or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We have testimony from some survivors saying that some victims were killed in hangars through having been beaten up with blunt objects. Brute force was applied with some blunt object, and these six people were killed through blows inflicted by blunt objects; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the cause of death, which we say trauma, trauma resulted in cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't have to be wary. I'm not asking you trick questions. I think you're a very proper expert witness, which is quite different to the ones we've heard previously. Anyway, one particular victim that was found, for that victim it was established that it had stab wounds on the body and neck. As far as I remember, and I studied the trial in Belgrade, the wound in Belgrade was inflicted from the back. It was a stab wound to the back of the neck, and the metal object entered the skull, right, pierced the skull? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to look at the autopsy report to see the direction, the channel stab, channel took, but certainly it was a result of a stab caused by a knife or whatever, and the injuries were inflicted that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you established that because the skull had been damaged by the stab wound. Had the person's neck been slit, it would be difficult for you to ascertain that; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, I have to look at the autopsy report. With that -- the particular person you're referring to, there was soft tissue present, so you could see the stab wound to the soft tissue in the neck. So the person conducting the autopsy saw the piercing of the skin and the channel the object took as it entered the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's a lot of material. I couldn't take it all with me, but I do remember that it was a bayonet or a knife that pierced the soft tissue through force. It is difficult for somebody wielding a knife to pierce the skull, unless he's very strong, but if it's a bayonet that was used, then it's easier to pierce the skull; right? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If the skull was damaged, then it had to be through great force and impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you found a number of stab wounds on the body, right, several? I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't do that, but the person conducting the autopsy found those injuries, stab wounds to the neck and torso, but there's no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I assume that all the autopsies were done with the intention of ascertaining the cause of death and that there was no manipulation there.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. We were there to monitor the whole process, and our colleagues from Serbia did the same, so there's no reason to doubt any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for these 200 victims, we agree that not a single one of them died through having their throat slit, without the use of firearms, without any stabbings and so on?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: What we can say is that the cause of death was ascertained. They were stab wounds, gunshot wounds, et cetera. Now, whether their throats were slit, that's difficult to establish because the tissue from the neck area was not described, because they disappeared. So there's no cause of death -- so a throat slitting was not listed as a cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you that, because we had a false witness here who claimed that several prisoners had their throat slit and died that way, without the use of firearms, in the liquidation process. That's why I found it important to clear that up in talking to you. Now, we have a great disproportion here in the number of cartridges found and bullets found. There are three times as many cartridges that were found than bullets, because many of the bullets didn't hit their target, they didn't hit the victim. So that is one possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting. I'm pausing slightly for the interpretation. If many more cartridges were found compared to bullets or gunshot wounds, then of course a part of those projectiles used went far off the mark, didn't hit their target. Now, the question is how many entrance/exit wounds were established. Perhaps the soft tissue was hit, which disintegrated later on, and so no traces were found during the autopsy and they weren't recorded. So it's difficult for me to give you an exact answer, but to all intents and purposes, the large number of cartridges found show perhaps that the bullets had either gone astray or that they had hit soft tissues which had disintegrated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused repeat his question, please. It was much too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the interpreters didn't catch your question because you're overlapping. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was suggesting to the witness is the following: I'm saying that it might be possible that certain projectiles cause entrance/exit wounds, which means they went through the body and continued along their trajectory and that those bullets were never found, so they could have been bullets that did not touch any of the bones, go through any of the bones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is possible, and in fact many bullets, whether they passed through soft tissues or some bones, might have exited the body and then, therefore, were never found. So that is something that happens, too, particularly in the case of Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We had the example of one woman -- there were two women who were killed, but with one of these victims, female victims, doctors, specialists ascertained that it wasn't possible that she had been pregnant because of her age. Now, as to the other woman, the other person, you yourself said that it wasn't possible to ascertain whether the person was pregnant or not because of putrifaction and decay. Now, if it was advanced pregnancy, for example, the fetus in its eighth month, for such an advanced pregnancy, would the same answer hold true, that it's not possible to establish whether someone is pregnant or not because of decay and putrifaction?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The description during the autopsy is quite clear and indicates that there were no visible signs of pregnancy. And I have to repeat once again, when we're dealing with pregnancy, even advanced pregnancy in the eighth or ninth months, the first thing that disappears in the process of decay is the fetus because, as I said, the fetus is made up 90 per cent of water, and so it is the fetus that disintegrates and dissolves and you cannot find it later on. So it is possible that somebody might have been in an advanced state of pregnancy and that this cannot be ascertained. And six years after death, it's quite possible that you can't find any traces which would have suggested that the person was pregnant, the woman was pregnant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this might be morbid, and since we're in open session, I'd like to ask you something, but this is important for me because of previous testimony by someone else. Is it possible, and you presented data about that, that on the body of that particular woman, a lot of entrance wounds were found all over her body and on her head? Is it possible that all those bullets, that the woman was reclining or semi-reclining and that all the bullets were shot -- well, if the woman was lying -- well, that all the bullets were shot into her genital area and that then they spread through the body and reached the head as well? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the description of the entrance/exit wound, quite obviously it was a burst of gunfire that went from top to bottom or bottom to top, from head down the body or the other way around, but there are no indices to show that everything was concentrated on the pelvic area, because she had been pierced all over her body; her head, her body and her pelvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, we know the woman's name. I don't think I'll bring that up in open session. But was she in the upright position when this burst of gunfire was shot at her and into her?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The wounds and injuries that are incurred from the head down the body to the extremities, as a rule, are inflicted on somebody in the upright position when there's a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Strinovic, I have one more question for you. The Serb that was killed in Vocin, Stojan Nenadovic was mentioned, and in my opinion, from quite clear morbid propaganda reasons, the Prosecutor chose to display that photograph. And then you said the man was killed because his son was in the Croatian Army. Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We received that information when we arrived in Slatina and started the autopsy and came to that particular body. Then we were given the information from the authorities who found the body in Slatina and -- well, we came across the body, and the officials there told us that he was a Serb whose son was in the Croatian Army and that that was the reason, so that's where we got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Croatian courts tried some of the perpetrators of the crimes in Vocin on the 13th of December? Do you know that there was a trial either in Bjelovar or Podravska Slatina, I think that was the relevant court or was it Podravska Slatina? I'm not quite sure now, I can't remember, but do you know that they were taken to court and tried?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, proceedings were initiated against certain perpetrators, certain individuals, and the investigating judge asked for an expert opinion which was then to serve for that trial linked to the victims of Vocin. Now, I don't know anything more than that, whether there was a judgement, whether they were sentenced or not. I don't know how the trial ended, but I do know that proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that all the accused in that trial were Vocin locals, local people from Vocin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I don't know all the details of the case, nor do I know who the perpetrators were, the accused were, so I don't know who was taken to trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then I assume that you don't know whether the trial incorporated or -- that the trial incorporated persons accused for the killing of the Serb Stojan Nenadovic.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: My answer would be the same as my previous answer. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But since you speculated on the basis of knowledge that you received -- information that you received from the people who brought in the corpse and who had heard something about the case, is my speculation possible, too, that this Serb didn't want to flee from Vocin when the rest of the Serbs withdrew and fled, with the onslaught of the Croatian Army and the police, and he remained because he considered because of the fact that his son was in the Croatian Army would mean that his life would be saved; however, the first Croatian forces that entered, they beat him up as a Serb, without listening to him saying that his son was a member of the Croatian Army? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said I have no specific or objective information, except what I heard when we arrived in Vocin. Of course, all options are open.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm glad that you said very fairly that you have no reliable data. I've just now constructed this speculation of mine, and I'm sure that you are quite clear on that, and that I did in response to this unfair proceeding on the part of the Prosecutor. Thank you, Mr. Strinovic. I think that you were a very fair witness and expert witness, but you might be called again once I have submitted this 50 pages of transcript that have not been translated. I am going to apply for it, Mrs. Lattanzi. You can, of course, not grant my application, but I will do so. You will probably not be called again, Mr. Strinovic, but I'm going to do so in order to teach the Prosecutor a lecture. Thank you, Mr. Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you answered one of Mr. Seselj's questions, you said you testified at the Ovcara trial in Belgrade, and you said that when I put the question to you right at the beginning of your testimony. I was wondering, when you testified in Belgrade, since you, as a forensic pathologist, you hadn't taken part in the examinations, forensic examinations, you were called to testify in what capacity; because you're a well-known expert? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were given a query and a summons from the court in Belgrade to come to the hearing and to prepare material related to the identification of the post-mortal remains, exclusively that identification, because I and Dr. Kubat worked on that identification. I did the classical part and he the DNA one. They were particularly interested to hear how we had established those names that we had identified, and how reliable our method was, and whether we were able to guarantee that identification was reliable. So it was exclusively for the purpose of the -- of our explaining how we had established that -- how we had identified the 192 bodies that we had identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I suppose that you were put questions by the judges, just as we put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but also solely in respect of the identification, not in connection with the cause of death or the history of the Ovcara gravesite from beginning to end. It was all solely pertaining to the identification method, the ante-mortem data strictly connected to identification. That was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, I just have one question regarding the information that you gave us on the size of the mass grave, because it struck me -- but I have no experience with this, but it struck me a bit odd that you would have room for 200 bodies in a single mass grave measuring 7 by 9 metres. How deep was it, or were there several mass graves at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was just one mass grave. All the bodies were in one place, in one heap. Now, what the height or the depth of the grave was, it is hard for me to say offhand, but it must have been at least five or six metres. It was an impressive depth of that mass grave, where there was a relatively small area but the depth was enough to accommodate 200 bodies, and they were piled up in a pyramidal heap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a couple of questions. Before that, I was just informed that we have the transcript -- the translation of the transcript that are missing ready by tomorrow afternoon. So if we want to keep the witness so he doesn't need to come back, if Mr. Seselj wants to continue his cross-examination after reading this transcript. And before that, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not believe that it is that relevant a point. Mr. Seselj, do you insist on reading that transcript, to then possibly ask further questions to the witness, or is that not necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What matters to me is that I get that portion of the transcript, because I'm entitled to it. Perhaps I am not going to use it in cross-examining Mr. Strinovic. Perhaps I'm going to use it at some other juncture in this place, in this trial. But if Mr. Ferrara guarantees that I'm going to get it tomorrow afternoon, Mr. Strinovic can have a happy journey back home. I'm not going to insist on cross-examining him. But today, when we finish, I'm going to raise an administrative matter, so will you please bear that in mind? It is very important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Ferrara, you will disclose the transcript to Mr. Ferrara [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, your report, we found that until now there are four cases, in four cases the cause of death of the people killed at Ovcara are unknown. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When it is established that the cause of death is unknown, unascertained, that means that either there have been no visible wounds or that it was the soft tissue that had been wounded. It could have been an exit-and-entry wound or slaughter or a gunshot wound, but because the soft tissue decays and dissolves with time, it is not possible to establish that. Then there could have been extensive damage to the skull or some other bones, but that damage cannot be reproduced. It cannot be associated with a gunshot wound, with a blow or something similar, so that in some cases the post-mortem examiner is not sure, having conducted all the necessary examinations, taking all the necessary steps, examining all the organs and tissues. The examiner is in a dilemma, cannot establish the actual cause, the real cause of death, in which case the indication is the cause of death, unknown. I suppose that's what happened in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: In the case of killing as consequences of stabbing, slaughtering, strangulation, is it always possible to prove the causes of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not. As I've just said, in such cases when we have strangulation, stabbing wounds and similar, and the damage was inflicted on soft tissue, and the soft tissue has decayed, completely dissolved because the bodies were in this surface layer or were changed -- or other changes took place, there is no indication of what wound really was inflicted on the soft tissue to indicate the cause of death, in which case the cause of death is unascertainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Strinovic, in such a case, in the case of a wound being inflicted to the soft tissues and the soft tissues being then decomposed, is it possible that these people died as a result of a haemorrhage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. When people have bled to death and then we have post-mortal damage to tissue, that is precisely when it is impossible to establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, we have just completed your testimony. On my behalf and on behalf of my colleagues, thank you very much for having come for the fourth time, I believe, to The Hague. Thank you very much for having assisted the Bench with your technical knowledge. I wish you every success in your occupation, and I wish you a safe trip home. And I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you said that you wanted to raise another matter. But before I give you the floor, let me turn to Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow, we have a witness whose name I'm not going to give because it's a protected witness. This witness will be here at a quarter past 2.00. Two hours have been given to the Prosecution to examine this witness, and two hours for Mr. Seselj to cross-examine him. That's right? Okay, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor, Ms. Dahl, but before I do, let me say the following: Mr. Seselj, you've developed your point, and you are asking the Chamber to take measures. The Trial Chamber may act proprio motu, but you also can file a motion. Is what you've just said tantamount to an oral motion? Should we see that as an oral motion from you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official oral application on my part. It is formulated succinctly, and -- but it is very precise. I did so in order to save time. I can give it in writing in a number of pages, but, yes, you can read this as my official oral motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, so am I to understand that you are asking the Chamber to initiate contempt proceedings against this witness for having done what exactly; falsely testified for having driven his car into a field, which is not possible, or, I mean, what's the substance of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, my request is that we go into private session and redact this information, because it's susceptible to being interpreted as witness intimidation, and it also relates to Rule 77. The redaction would begin at today's transcript page 90, line 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely oppose that, because I think that that would be an outrage. I strictly -- took strict care that no one can even guess the identity of this witness, no one on earth, so if you are going to redact this and move into private session, please consider this motion not having been made, because I've had enough of private sessions, really. Then I could be strangulated in the dark here or I could be strangulated in public. I opt for the second possibility. I'm not threatening anyone here, but if the moment is ripe for instituting proceedings for contempt of court against one witness, that is not intimidation of other witnesses. One has been caught shamefacedly lying. What happens if we catch a witness lying and I want proceedings to be instituted against him? How can that amount to intimidation of other witnesses? This is only a message to other witnesses to speak the truth and not falsely testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has been requested to redact part of the transcript, and I have to consult my colleagues before we make our determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, after considering the matter -- but before saying anything else, let's go into private session. Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00. We are going to be hearing a witness who has been granted protective measures. I wish you a pleasant evening, and we meet again tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
